content.title: Gaussian distribution pooling for MIL
content.review:
**Summary:**

This paper analyzes pooling functions for Multiple Instance Learning (MIL). The authors presented and compared several point estimate and distribution pooling functions. They also showed some theoretical properties of some point estimate and Gaussian distribution based poolings. They extended the Gaussian distribution pooling with an attention mechanism. Finally, they analyzed empirically 5 pooling functions on a lymph node metastases dataset.

**Reasons for score:** 

Overall, I feel it is quite difficult to evaluate the quality/impact of this paper because a lot of parts are not well motivated. For example, the authors show some theoretical results but never explain why these results are important. The comparison to some existing pooling functions is missing.

**Pros:**

- The introduction section to the MIL framework is easy to understand.
- I think the idea of using a Gaussian distribution pooling for MIL is novel.
- I like the idea to compare the pooling functions in several contexts.
- MIL models are an interesting direction because they allow to reduce the annotation complexity.

**Cons:**

First, I think the term distribution pooling is quite confusing because it is specific to a Gaussian distribution pooling. I think the authors should rename it to something like Gaussian distribution pooling. The authors used the term distribution based pooling in the title and abstract so the reader can think that it will present results for generic distribution based pooling but the paper only shows results about Gaussian distribution based pooling. The authors should be clearer about what is in this paper. 

The technical contribution of the distribution with attention pooling is very limited. It is a straightforward extension of the distribution pooling where the attention is computed with a softmax. The authors did not explain the motivation of the distribution with attention pooling. Attention models are trendy but it is not enough to justify a new pooling  function. For example, the authors should explain what problem the distribution pooling cannot solve but the distribution with attention pooling can. It will help to understand the importance/impact of this contribution.

In the abstract and the contribution section, the authors claim that  they “theoretically showed that the distribution based pooling filters are superior to the point estimate based counterparts.” I did not see where it is proved in the paper. In general, it is not a good idea to say that something is better than something else without giving detail. The authors should specify the metric or for what property. There are a lot of ways to evaluate/compare a model: metric (accuracy), stability, convergence speed, robustness (noise, adversarial attack), fairness, runtime, etc. 

The authors did not explain the importance of their theoretical results. For example, it is difficult to understand why the property 1 (“given two feature matrices, whenever ‘max’ pooling filter produces two different representations, so does ‘distribution’ pooling filter”) is important. If the goal is to classify the bags, this property does not seem important. In a perfect world, you only need 2 representations: one for the positive bags and one for the negative bags. The authors should also explain what is a perfect filter (proposition 2 and 3).

I think some comparisons to pooling functions are missing. The authors did not compare their model with [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. I know three are a lot of papers about MIL and it is not possible to compare with every approach but I think the authors should at least compare with [5] because it is a generalization of a lot of pooling functions and the deep set paper [6].

It is a bit difficult to understand some results of table 3. For example in the 3-class scenario, there is almost a 3pt difference between the distribution and the attention poolings but the difference is not significant (p>0.05). The authors show results on a new dataset so it is quite challenging to understand the difficulty of the task. There are a lot of existing MIL datasets so the authors should justify why they need a new dataset or why they cannot use existing MIL datasets. However, the idea to compare pooling functions for different tasks is interesting  but it will be better if it is on well-known datasets.
They show results on very old MIL datasets but I do not think they are the right datasets to evaluate the model because they are very small datasets and can be sensible to the random seed. For example, it is quite difficult to interpret the results of 0.923 on MIUSK1 because the result was 0.874 20 year ago when the mi/MI-SVM paper was published. I think this paper will be stronger if the authors show results on bigger and more recent dataset like MSCOCO (see [6]). 

**Minor comment:**

I think there is room to improve the structure and some notations in the paper. For instance, I do not think that the distribution with attention pooling should be in the MIL framework section because it is a technical contribution. It should have its own section with its motivation. I think it is possible to replace $f_{x_i}^j$ by standard matrix notation $F_{x_i, j}$ because F is a feature matrix. Also the notation $[...|...]$ is not consistent because it creates a vector and a matrix. 

[1]  Lee C., Gallagher PW., Tu Z. Generalizing Pooling Functions in Convolutional Neural Networks: Mixed, Gated, and Tree. In AISTATS, 2016.

[2] Sun C., Paluri M., Collobert R., Nevatia R., Bourdev L. ProNet: Learning to Propose Object-specific Boxes for Cascaded Neural Networks. In CVPR, 2016.

[3] Girdhar R., Ramanan D. Attentional Pooling for Action Recognition. In NeurIPS, 2017.

[4] Kulkarni, Jurie, Zepeda, Perez, Chevallier. SPLeaP: Soft Pooling of Learned Parts for Image Classification. In ECCV, 2016.

[5] Diane Bouchacourt, Sebastian Nowozin, M. Pawan Kumar. Entropy-Based Latent Structured Output Prediction. In ICCV, 2015.

[6] Zaheer, Manzil and Kottur, Satwik and Ravanbakhsh, Siamak and Poczos, Barnabas and Salakhutdinov, Ruslan R and Smola, Alexander J. Deep Sets. In NeurIPS, 2017.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Authors' Response to Reviewer 1, part 1
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your valuable time, insightful comments and suggestions. Please find our answers to your questions below. We have updated our paper based on suggestions and comments of the reviewers. The summary of updates in the paper are listed in a separate comment on top of the page. If you have any further comments or suggestions on the updated version of our paper, we will be glad to improve on them. Thanks.

1\) "I think the term distribution pooling is quite confusing because it is specific to a Gaussian distribution pooling. [...]"

--> We apologize for misunderstanding. For clarification, marginal distributions estimated by 'distribution' pooling filter don't have to be Gaussian distributions.

2\)  "[...] The authors did not explain the motivation of the distribution with attention pooling. [...]"

--> We have updated Sec. 2.1.2 to better express the motivation behind 'distribution with attention' pooling filter. Please see Sec. 2.1.2 for details. 

In MIL, all instances inside a bag may not contribute equally to the bag label. In such cases, it is important to prioritize some of the instances inside the bag. For example, in positive vs negative bag classification task, even one 'positive' instance makes a bag 'positive' and it is crucial to capture this instance. In 'distribution with attention' pooling, our motivation is to address such cases by associating an attention weight with each instance.

3\) "the authors claim that they “theoretically showed that the distribution based pooling filters are superior to the point estimate based counterparts.” I did not see where it is proved in the paper. [...]"

--> We stated Proposition 1, 2, 3 in Sec. 2.2 and gave the proofs in Supp. A. Please see Supp. A for the proofs.

4\) "The authors did not explain the importance of their theoretical results. For example, it is difficult to understand why the property 1 (“given two feature matrices, whenever ‘max’ pooling filter produces two different representations, so does ‘distribution’ pooling filter”) is important. [...]"

--> We have updated Sec 2.2 to better explain the importance of our theoretical findings. Please see Sec. 2.2 for details. 

Proposition 1, for example, states that: whenever two bags from different classes are discriminated by 'max' pooling, they are also discriminated by 'distribution' pooling. However, converse of the Proposition 1 is not true. There are cases that two bags from different classes are discriminated by 'distribution' pooling, but they are not discriminated by 'max' pooling.

5\) "The authors should also explain what is a perfect filter (proposition 2 and 3)."

--> Perfect filter assumption was related to standard deviation of Gaussian kernel ($\sigma$) in 'distribution' pooling filter; however we have realized that it is not necessary for this set of propositions. So, we have updated the propositions accordingly in Sec. 2.2 and Supp. A. Please see Sec. 2.2 and Supp. A.

6\) "The comparison to some existing pooling functions is missing. [...]"

--> In this paper, we have included 'max', 'mean' and 'attention' pooling as basic point estimate based pooling filters. Actually, the other point estimate based pooling filters, including the ones mentioned by the reviewers, either can be written in terms of these basic ones or they are the "subsets" of them.
 - 'Sum' pooling (Zaheer et al., 2017) is the scaled version of 'mean' pooling by N (N: number of instances in a bag).
 - 'Exponential softmax' pooling (Wang et al., 2019) is a special version of 'attention' pooling with attention neural network being 'identity' mapping.
 - 'Top-k instance' pooling (Li et al., 2015) is equivalent to 'max' pooling for k=1 and 'mean' pooling for k=N (N: number of instances in a bag).

7\) "It is a bit difficult to understand some results of table 2. For example in the 3-class scenario, there is almost a 3pt difference between the distribution and the attention poolings but the difference is not significant ($p>0.05$)."

--> Please see Supp. B.3 for further details about the performance of the models. We have added confusion matrices of classification tasks in Supp. B.3 to provide readers with more details about performance of the models.

content.comment:
8\) "The authors show results on a new dataset so it is quite challenging to understand the difficulty of the task. There are a lot of existing MIL datasets so the authors should justify why they need a new dataset or why they cannot use existing MIL datasets. [...]"

--> In this paper, we used two datasets both from literature: Classical MIL datasets (MUSK datasets of Dietterich et al. (1997) and Animal datasets of Andrews et al. (2003)) and Lymph node metastases dataset of Oner et al. (2020). 

We used classical MIL datasets due to historical reasons since almost all of the mil pooling papers used those datasets for comparison (see Table 3). Although they are quite small in the context of deep learning as highlighted by the reviewers, they are still used even in recent papers like 'attention' pooling paper of Ilse et al. (2018).

On the other, in order to present a more realistic analysis, we used lymph node metastases dataset of Oner et al. (2020), which is a real world biomedical image dataset with weak labels. We preferred this dataset in our analysis since it has already been tested with 'distribution' pooling filter on 'ucc' task in Oner et al. (2020) and it is much larger than many of the medical image datasets used in mil papers, such as Breast (58 images) and Colon (100 images) cancer datasets used in Ilse et al. (2018).

content.title: Paper is an easy read, however, it lacks a good theoretical foundation
content.review:
**Summary of the paper**
* The paper proposes a categorization of Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) criterion into point estimate (mean, max etc.) and distribution based representation of bags.
* A distribution based representation for a bag is supposed to be superior in some sense and hence, the paper claims that it should provide a better performance than the point estimate based representation.
* The paper extends the previously proposed kernel density based MIL criterion in Oner et al, 2020 with the concept of attention using weights. It also includes theoretical analysis of some of the properties of the distribution based filters.
* The experiments are performed on a lymph node metastases dataset where the images have to be classified as being normal, metastases or boundary/mixed. There are also experiments performed with classical MIL datasets on drug activity prediction and animal image annotation. The results are mixed in terms of the superiority of the proposed distribution with attention representation.

**Strengths**
* The inclusion of attention in the distribution filter is a nice way to extend and round out the work of Oner et al. 2020.
* The experiments with the lymph node metastases dataset are performed for five different types of MIL tasks while comparing five different pooling filters on each task. The results provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the different MIL filters on the different tasks.
* The code is made available.

**Weaknesses**
* The distribution filter as proposed in this work uses a kernel density estimator to sample the distribution uniformly along the different dimensions. I am not really sure if we can still call the sampled representation a distribution function. Consider an alternative viewpoint to the framework depicted in Figure 1 where \\(\theta_{transform}\\) absorbs the max, mean, attention pooling. This can be achieved as part of the \\(\theta_{transform}\\) by making the first layer be max-pooling, average pooling or a single linear layer applied on the feature dimension. The \\(\theta_{filter}\\) would then just be an identity mapping after feature extraction for the max, mean and attention pooling filters, whereas it would be the density based representation for the distribution filter. The module \\(\theta_{transform}\\) has the freedom to incorporate attention pooling on the new features and then follow it up with a multi-layer perceptron for final classification.
* The theoretical analysis as provided in the propositions 1-3 is mostly about the properties of distributions. I was not able to understand why these serve as a theoretical justification for the “superiority” of them over point estimates. The theoretical analysis did not provide insight into why such a “superiority” leads to better performance on the task at hand. The statement in contribution 2 - “distributed with attention pooling filter is theoretically the best” is not fully justified because the term “best” is not defined and its relevance to the final classification performance is not provided.
* In the proof for proposition 3, the density function in subsection (ii) is expressed in terms of \\(g_{x_i}\\) which is a weighted feature value \\(w_i f_{x_i}\\). I was not able to understand why the distribution filter was written in terms of this. If I understand correctly the default distribution filter works directly on the features \\(f_{x_i}\\). If the features are multiplied by those “attention weights” then it is incorrect to refer to it as \\(p_X\\) anymore. The set \\(X\\) is now different due to the weighting. Hence, I believe the proof is not valid. Please correct me if I am missing something.
* If the distribution based bag representation is the best and superior according to the theoretical analysis, the experimental results don’t reflect that. It seems like the mean pooling can be better in a multi-task setting as shown in Table 2.
* It isn’t clear if the Distribution-Net as labeled in Table 3 uses attention or not. Table 3 should probably also include the results from all the five MIL filters. It will be good to see information about the differences in the feature extraction network between Distribution-Net and the baselines like Wang et al., 2018 and Ilse et al., 2018.
* Similarly, the results in Table 2 on the lymph node metastases dataset are missing comparisons to a baseline method from literature.

**Questions/Minor comments**
* It is easy to follow the paper, however, there are some minor issues in the writing which can be improved. Ex: Second paragraph in page 2: The sentence starting with “We theoretically showed” should probably be in present tense. The second half of “However, they don’t go beyond one specific application and lack of theoretical analysis” needs some grammatical correction.
* Are there any insights into the performance of the distribution filter when the bag size is small? Why was it fixed to 64 in the experiments? Would a large number help in better estimation of the distribution?

**Justification of rating**
The paper’s claims of a novel categorization of MIL filters, incorporating attention into distribution based representation and the theoretical analysis fall short in various ways as mentioned in the weaknesses.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Authors' Response to Reviewer 4, part 1
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your valuable time, insightful comments and suggestions. Please find our answers to your questions below. We have updated our paper based on suggestions and comments of the reviewers. The summary of updates in the paper are listed in a separate comment on top of the page. If you have any further comments or suggestions on the updated version of our paper, we will be glad to improve on them. Thanks.

1\) "The distribution filter as proposed in this work uses a kernel density estimator to sample the distribution uniformly along the different dimensions. I am not really sure if we can still call the sampled representation a distribution function."

--> Estimated marginal distributions are uniformly binned during training neural network models for computational purposes. The representation obtained as a result of binning is a 'probability mass function' or 'discrete probability distribution'.

2\) "Consider an alternative viewpoint to the framework depicted in Figure 1 where $\theta_{transform}$ absorbs the max, mean, attention pooling. [...]"

--> We agree with the reviewer. It is possible to combine $\theta_{filter}$ and $\theta_{transform}$ modules to achieve the same thing. In theory, neural networks are universal function approximators and we can include one big neural network instead of all three modules as well. However, this raises well-known problems already discussed in detail in the literature such as difficulty in optimization, overfitting, loss of ability in including domain knowledge in network design, etc.

3\) "The theoretical analysis as provided in the propositions 1-3 is mostly about the properties of distributions. I was not able to understand why these serve as a theoretical justification for the “superiority” of them over point estimates. [...]"

The reviewer is correct, we have used the properties of distributions for our proofs. Indeed, this is the powerful part of distribution based pooling filters over point estimate based pooling filters: they can exploit the information in the distributions rather than looking at point statistics.

We have also updated Sec 2.2 (theoretical analysis part) to better explain the importance of our theoretical findings better. Please see Sec. 2.2 for details.

Proposition 1, for example, states that: whenever two bags from different classes are discriminated by 'max' pooling, they are also discriminated by 'distribution' pooling. However, converse of the Proposition 1 is not true. There are cases that two bags from different classes are discriminated by 'distribution' pooling, but they are not discriminated by 'max' pooling.

4\) "The statement in contribution 2 - "distribution with attention pooling filter is theoretically the best" is not fully justified because the term "best" is not defined and its relevance to the final classification performance is not provided."

We apologize for not being clear. We have updated contribution 2 and other necessary parts in the paper by specifying that "distribution based pooling filters are superior to their point estimate based counterparts **in terms of amount of information captured while obtaining bag level representations from extracted features**". Similarly, the relevance to final performance is that: bag level representations containing more information helps to improve the performance on the task at hand.

5\) "In the proof for proposition 3, the density function in subsection (ii) is expressed in terms of $g_{x_i}$ which is a weighted feature value $w_if_{x_i}$. I was not able to understand why the distribution filter was written in terms of this. [...]"

--> Proposition 3 shows that bag level representation obtained by 'attention' pooling filter can be fully recovered from bag level representation obtained by 'distribution' pooling filter by using the given feature matrix and attention weights. The set $X$ and 'distribution' pooling filter do not change in here, only difference is that 'distribution' pooling filter gets weighted feature vectors as input, as the reviewer highlighted. Given conditions of the proposition are satisfied, the proof is valid.

replying_to: Replying to Authors' Response to Reviewer 4, part 1

content.title: Authors' Response to Reviewer 4, part 2
content.comment:
6\) "If the distribution based bag representation is the best and superior according to the theoretical analysis, the experimental results don’t reflect that. It seems like the mean pooling can be better in a multi-task setting as shown in Table 2."

--> Theoretical analysis is based on the assumption that feature extractor modules are identical for different pooling filters. This is why all propositions are conditioned on "given the feature matrices" and proved based on that. On the other hand, during the experiments, all the models were initialized from scratch and trained end-to-end as in real world. So, the models with different pooling filter modules potentially had different feature extractor modules. Therefore, it is possible that the feature extractor of the model with 'mean' pooling filter might extract better features and gave slightly better results than the models with distribution based pooling filters. However, this does not contradict with our theoretical analysis. Still, we can use Proposition 2: by using the feature extractor of the model with 'mean' pooling filter we can obtain a model with a distribution based pooling filter that gives at least as good results as the model with 'mean' pooling filter in the "Normal" task of multi-task setting.

7\) "It isn’t clear if the Distribution-Net as labeled in Table 3 uses attention or not. Table 3 should probably also include the results from all the five MIL filters. It will be good to see information about the differences in the feature extraction network between Distribution-Net and the baselines like Wang et al., 2018 and Ilse et al., 2018."

--> Distribution-Net has 'distribution' pooling and does not use attention. We tested our model only with 'distribution' pooling filter as a baseline in distribution based pooling filters group. Other pooling filters ('max', 'mean' and 'attention') were already tested in Wang et al. (2018) and Ilse et al. (2018) and included in the Table 3.

The details of the architectures used in Wang et al. (2018) and Ilse et al. (2018) are included in Table 9 in Supp. C. Please see Supp. C.

8\) "Similarly, the results in Table 2 on the lymph node metastases dataset are missing comparisons to a baseline method from literature."

--> We haven't included traditional machine learning based methods in Table 2 since our proposed framework is neural network based and it has already been shown that traditional machine learning based methods are mostly outperformed by neural network based methods. On the other hand, we have included 'max', 'mean' and 'attention' pooling filters of Wang et al. (2018) and Ilse et al. (2018) in our experiments.

9\) "Are there any insights into the performance of the distribution filter when the bag size is small? Why was it fixed to 64 in the experiments? Would a large number help in better estimation of the distribution?"

--> The number of instances in a bag should be large enough to capture the "necessary" information in an image to be able to make correct decision. Obviously, with very few patches, there is no way to capture the "necessary" information in an image, so the performances of all filters will drop substantially. However, once a certain threshold is exceeded, 'distribution' pooling filter is quite robust to the number of patches in a bag (see Supp. D). On the other hand, when we increase the number of instances in a bag a lot, it does not bring additional value yet put computation burden on network. So, a proper value must be chosen, ideally with cross validation on validation set. For classical MIL datasets, we have determined number of instances with cross-validation on the validation sets. For the lymph node metastases dataset, we used the value of 32 instances per bag in Oner et al. (2020) as basis and increased it to 64 in order to be on the safe side.

We have included a small section in Supp. D. There are some insights related to effect of number of instances in a bag on the performance of a model. Please see Supp. D for details.

10\) "It is easy to follow the paper, however, there are some minor issues in the writing which can be improved. [...]"

--> Thanks for highlighting these issues, we have updated the paper accordingly.

content.title: Clarification for proof of Proposition 3
content.comment:
The marginal distribution $\tilde p_X^{j}(v)$ as defined in Eqn (1) is not the same as in Section (ii) of the proof for Proposition 3. The $f_{x_i}^j$ in Eqn (1) is not interchangeable with $g_{x_i}^j$ because of the relationship $g_{x_i}^j=w_if_{x_i}^j$.

For a given feature representation $f_{x_i}^j$, the attention and distribution filters are defined as below (taken from the text of the main paper).

${ }_{att}h^j_X = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i f_{x_i}^j$ (A)

and 

$V^j = \tilde p_X^{j}(v)$

$ = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\(v - f_{x_i}^j\)^2}$ (B)

If we want to change the feature representation to $g_{x_i}$, then we should update both the filter equations above. This gives us

${ }_{att}h^j_X = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i g_{x_i}^j$ (C)

and 

$V^j = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\(v - g_{x_i}^j\)^2}$ (D)

I am unable to follow the proof since it shows a relationship between the filter in Eqn. A and the filter in Eqn. D which are not for the same feature representation. Could you elaborate on what Proposition 3 is trying to convey and the need for it?

replying_to: Replying to Clarification for proof of Proposition 3
display_title: Clarification on the proof of Proposition 3

content.title: Clarification on the proof of Proposition 3
content.comment:
We agree with the reviewer that in the proof of proposition 3 'attention' pooling operates on $f_{x_i}^{j}$ and 'distribution' pooling operates on $g_{x_i}^{j}= w_if_{x_i}^{j}$. Moreover, $B \neq D$ as the reviewer highlighted.

$\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi{\sigma}^2}} e^{-\frac{1}{2{\sigma}^2} \left(v- f_{x_i}^{j}\right)^2}$ (B)

$\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi{\sigma}^2}} e^{-\frac{1}{2{\sigma}^2} \left(v- w_if_{x_i}^{j}\right)^2}$ (D) 

 If it would be more convenient, it is possible to consider Eqn. D as another variant of 'distribution' pooling which scales the input feature vectors with weights $w_i$'s first and then obtain marginal distributions. Yet, the main point of Proposition 3 does not change: given the feature matrix and attention weights, bag level representation obtained by 'attention' pooling filter can be fully recovered from bag level representation obtained by (the variant of) 'distribution' pooling filter.

display_title: An OK paper that extends two previous works for MIL.

content.title: An OK paper that extends two previous works for MIL.
content.review:
Methodology:
The paper presents an approach for MIL. Two previous pooling operators (attention and distribution) are combined to capture more information with the attention scores and raw instance-level score. Some theoretical results were provided to support the claim of information gain in the proposed operator. Experiments on two benchmarks show that the attention-distribution operator outperforms four baseline MIL pooling operators.       
            
Pros:
The paper combines two pooling operators in a reasonable way to achieve better empirical results.  

Cons:
- The overall conceptual and technical novelty is limited.
The work basically extends two existing MIL pooling operators (attention and distribution) in a straightforward and trivial fashion, which does not provide much more insights into the problem itself. The marginal contribution does not justify the significance well.     

- Three propositions are presented to justify the information superiority between pooling operators. The statements and proves are always based on conditions that “f attention weights are accessible and pooling filters θfilter and θfilter are perfect,”, so what is a perfect filter exactly in this context? 

- Empirical study should be enhanced
For one thing, several other interesting popular pooling operators or strategies are not tested. , To name a few, the linear softmax and exponential softmax pooling operators from “A Comparison of Five Multiple Instance Learning Pooling Functions for Sound Event Detection with Weak Labeling” ICASSP 2019, the top-k instance pooling operator from “Multiple instance learning for soft bags via top instances”, CVPR 2015. These are also shown to outperform conventional max/mean/median pooling for MIL too.
Another concern is on the benchmarks. The two datasets used in the paper are not large enough (<3k examples) given today’s deep model context as adopted by the method. It would be great if the comparison on some more realistic benchmarks (E.g., MS COCO) can be presented too. Will that change the observations in the paper? Will a stronger / better-tuned attention affect the results and conclusion. Since the conceptual and technical novelty is limited, extensive empirical justification is needed for a more convincing conclusion.  


Minor comments:
It looks to me that some notations in the theoretical analysis need to be reconsidered. E.g. Proposition 2 mean h_X = E[dist h_X] does not make much sense to me. What is the expectation of a pdf (dist h_x) here? It looks like it should be E[v]~p(v) with p(v) from dist h_X.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

We used classical MIL datasets due to historical reasons since almost all of the mil pooling papers used those datasets for comparison (see Table 3). Although they are quite small in the context of deep learning as highlighted by the reviewers, they are still used even in recent papers like 'attention' pooling paper of Ilse et al. (2018).

On the other, in order to present a more realistic analysis, we used lymph node metastases dataset of Oner et al. (2020), which is a real world biomedical image dataset with weak labels. We preferred this dataset in our analysis since it has already been tested with 'distribution' pooling filter on 'ucc' task in Oner et al. (2020) and it is much larger than many of the medical image datasets used in mil papers, such as Breast (58 images) and Colon (100 images) cancer datasets used in Ilse et al. (2018).

5\) "[...] some notations in the theoretical analysis need to be reconsidered. [...]"

--> Thanks for pointing out this point. We have revised the notation in Sec. 2.2 and Supp. A as suggested. Please see Sec. 2.2 and Supp. A.

[1] Manzil Zaheer, Satwik Kottur, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, Barnabas Poczos, Ruslan R Salakhutdinov, and Alexander J Smola. Deep sets. In Advances in neural information processing systems, pp. 3391–3401, 2017.

[2] Yun Wang, Juncheng Li, and Florian Metze. A comparison of five multiple instance learning pooling functions for sound event detection with weak labeling. In ICASSP 2019-2019 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP), pp. 31–35. IEEE, 2019.

[3] Li, Weixin, and Nuno Vasconcelos. Multiple instance learning for soft bags via top instances. In Proceedings of the ieee conference on computer vision and pattern recognition, pp. 4277-4285. 2015.

content.title: Summary of updates in the paper
content.comment:
The updates made in the paper during rebuttal period are summarised in here!

- We have updated Sec. 2.1.2 to better express the advantages of distribution based pooling filters and the motivation behind `distribution with attention' pooling filter.

- We have updated Sec. 2.2 to clarify the importance of theoretical analysis and revised the notation as suggested by reviewers.

- We have added Table 9 into Supp. C to include model architectures used in Wang et al. (2018) and Ilse et al. (2018) on MUSK and Animal datasets.

- We have added confusion matrices of classification tasks in Supp. B.3 to provide readers with more details about performance of the models.

- We have included a small section in Supp. D to emphasize the advantages of distribution based pooling filters over point estimate based ones on a simple controlled toy example. There are also some insights related to effect of number of instances in a bag on the performance of a model.

[1] Xinggang Wang, Yongluan Yan, Peng Tang, Xiang Bai, and Wenyu Liu. Revisiting multiple instance neural networks. Pattern Recognition, 74:15–24, 2018.

[2] Maximilian Ilse, Jakub Tomczak, and Max Welling. Attention-based deep multiple instance learning. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 2127–2136, 2018.
